items.title: 66600_Teddy Wilson oral history interview
items.q: Dorothy Donzgan was around there, a young kid from Chicago

ctx.x: And then the other thing that always impressed me, the pianist Erroll Garner used to say -- Garner came up in the bebop movement with Charlie Parker and Dizzy and all those guys dominated, on 52nd Street, and the piano players of that period like Bud Powell, Al Haig -- and Dorothy Donzgan was around there, a young kid from Chicago, and George Shearing came from England, and Erroll Garner came from Pittsburgh, and Erroll didn't get swallowed up in that movement like a lot of them did. It was confused. Erroll just…
Before he died, he was the highest priced jazz piano player there was.

items.title: Dorothy Donegan — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: So, I played against Thelma Carpenter and Teddy Wilson.

ctx.x: ’54.’55. George Gewee (?) said I called and asked for the job, you know. So, he gave me $500, I said, “Oh, I’ll make this due.” He said, “Oh, you gotta pay your men out of it.” I said, “That’s alright too.” So, I played against Thelma Carpenter and Teddy Wilson. And Thelma
Carpenter took all the time. I said, “You can take all night, it ain’t gonna make no difference.” So I got on there and stopped that show cold.
